applicable_rules.text: A driver must drive a sufficient distance behind a vehicle travelling in front of the driver so the driver can, if necessary, stop safely to avoid a collision with the vehicle.

reasoning_chain.legal_principle: A falling TTC is the aggravating dynamic signal under the framework; its total absence here argues against escalation beyond a straightforward Rule 126 following-distance breach.

reasoning_chain.claim: Both vehicles are standard cars (4.6m), below the 7.5m long-vehicle threshold, so Rule 127's fixed 60m/200m minimum does not engage regardless of road/overtaking exemptions.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Rule 127 applies only to long vehicles (>=7.5m); neither vehicle meets this definition here.

aggravating_factors.factor: Night driving increases the required stopping-distance buffer, and the observed following distance fell short of that elevated standard for most of the segment.
Safe-T-Cam enforcement zone, meaning this segment is specifically the type of location NSW targets for following-distance enforcement.

mitigating_factors.factor: No sustained or falling TTC - the follower was not on an active closing/collision trajectory; gap was in fact widening over the latter half of the segment as lead accelerated away.

Dry road surface and clear calibration (RMSE 0.018m) reduce confidence that the distance readings themselves are in error, but also confirm conditions were not compounded by wet/gravel surface hazard.
Segment shows an initial settling period (gap_s 3.7-8.9s) before tightening, suggesting this may be a merge/gap-closing adjustment rather than deliberate tailgating throughout.

verdict.counterfactual: If sustained_below_4s_seconds (or sustained_clearance_below_3s_seconds) had been under ~2s rather than 4.45s - i.e., a brief post-merge dip rather than near-continuous sub-threshold following - the transiency doctrine would apply and the verdict would flip to unlikely_breach.
verdict.explanation_for_lay_user: The camera data shows this driver followed the car ahead with less clear road space than NSW recommends for night driving (at least 4 seconds) for almost the entire 5-second clip, with the clear-road gap dropping as low as about 1.2 seconds at one point. However, the following car was not actively closing in on the lead car - in fact the gap was widening by the end - so this looks like sustained close following rather than a dangerous high-speed pursuit. Based on this, a Rule 126 insufficient-following-distance penalty notice is the likely outcome, not a more serious dangerous-driving charge. Note that vehicle lengths here (4.6m) are too short for the long-vehicle Rule 127 minimum-distance rule to apply.

verdict.headline: Night-time following at 1.8-2.7s clearance, sustained ~87% of a 5.1s segment, breaches Rule 126's 4s night threshold.

applicable_rules.reason: Follower car tracked behind lead car on a night-time motorway with clearance_s/gap_s persistently under the applicable safe-following calibration for most of the observed segment.
applicable_rules.text: A driver must drive a sufficient distance behind a vehicle travelling in front of the driver so the driver can, if necessary, stop safely to avoid a collision with the vehicle.

evidence_assessment.summary: Both vehicles are 4.6 m cars, so Rule 127 (long-vehicle minimum distance) is not engaged. Rule 126 is assessed primarily via clearance_s: mean 2.022 s and median 1.798 s are well below the night-condition 4+ second calibration, and the segment spent 4.45 of 5.1 s (about 87%) below 3 s clearance. The less-strict gap_s metric (which folds in the follower's own body length) tells the same story at night - mean 2.734 s, with 4.45 s spent below the 4 s night threshold - so the two conventions converge on breach here despite normally diverging.

key_statistics.interpretation: Average clear-road time well under the 4 s night calibration; indicates insufficient stopping buffer for most of the segment.
More than half of samples show under 2 s of clear road ahead, consistent with sustained close-following, not a momentary dip.
Worst-case clearance observed; far below any applicable threshold, day or night.
87% of the 5.1 s segment was below 3 s clearance - satisfies the transiency doctrine's sustained-breach criterion even on the day-time 3 s test, let alone the stricter night 4 s test.
Using the less-strict rear-to-rear gap_s metric, the segment still spent 4.45 s below the night-appropriate 4 s threshold - confirms breach regardless of metric choice.
Negligible measurement noise in the gap/time figures themselves, supporting reliability of the distance-based findings.
No sustained active closing was detected; this is steady close-following rather than an acute collision-course event, which tempers escalation.

sample_citations.claim: Early in the segment clearance_s was already only 2.26 s, below the night 4 s calibration.
Minimum observed clearance_s of 1.17 s, the most severe single-sample deficit in the segment.
Even as lead vehicle pulled away (lead 62.4 km/h vs follower 31.7 km/h), clearance_s had only recovered to 2.81 s, still under night threshold.

event_citations.legal_significance: Lead vehicle decelerated by 6.7 km/h while follower clearance was still only ~2.8 s - demonstrates real-world risk reduction margin was compressed exactly when lead braked.
Second lead deceleration (7.6 km/h drop) shortly after the first, reinforcing that sustained short clearance left little buffer against lead speed variability.

perception_caveats: Speeds are vision-tracked estimates, not speedometer readings; follower/lead speeds should be treated as +/- a few km/h.
4 of 95 samples excluded for low confidence (0 excluded for out-of-range); excluded samples could not be checked and are a genuine gap in the record.
Night lighting conditions may reduce detection/tracking reliability generally, even though no explicit camera warnings were raised and calibration_rmse_m is very low (0.018 m).

gap_s and clearance_s diverge by design (gap_s includes follower body length); at night both converge toward breach here, but the choice of convention is noted per policy rather than silently resolved.

reasoning_chain.claim: Rule 126 is engaged because a following relationship between two cars was tracked with usable, high-confidence distance/time data for 5.1 s.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Rule 126 requires sufficient distance to stop safely; sufficiency is assessed via time-based following calibration.

reasoning_chain.claim: Night conditions trigger the stricter 4+ second calibration rather than the 3 second day-time calibration.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: NSW sufficiency calibration: 4+ seconds in poor conditions including night.

reasoning_chain.claim: clearance_s (the governing, stricter metric) shows mean 2.022 s and median 1.798 s, both substantially below the 4 s night threshold.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Clearance_s reflects true clear road ahead and is the preferred reading of the time-gap rule.

reasoning_chain.claim: The deficit was sustained, not transient: sustained_clearance_below_3s_seconds = 4.45 s out of a 5.1 s segment (~87%).
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Transiency doctrine: sustained_below_3s_seconds >= 5 s strongly supports breach in good conditions; here the proportion of the segment affected is even higher, and conditions are worse than 'good' (night).

reasoning_chain.claim: The less strict gap_s metric, re-tested against the correct night threshold of 4 s (not 3 s), also shows sustained breach: sustained_below_4s_seconds = 4.45 s of 5.1 s.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Where gap_s and clearance_s converge on breach under the condition-appropriate threshold, the measurement-convention uncertainty does not materially affect the verdict.

reasoning_chain.claim: No sustained TTC closing hazard was recorded (ttc_s null throughout, seconds_closing = 0.0), indicating steady close-following rather than an acute collision-course.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: A falling/low TTC would aggravate toward dangerous driving; its absence here limits escalation.

reasoning_chain.claim: Two lead_brake events near the end of the segment occurred while clearance was still under the night threshold, modestly aggravating the risk profile even though no TTC spike was captured.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Real-world braking variability by the lead vehicle tests whether the following distance was in fact sufficient to stop safely, per Rule 126's text.

reasoning_chain.claim: Rule 127 does not apply because both vehicles are 4.6 m cars, well under the 7.5 m long-vehicle threshold.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Rule 127 requires both vehicles to be 'long vehicles'; this condition is not met.

aggravating_factors.factor: Night conditions elevate the required following time to 4+ seconds, a threshold the follower failed to meet for most of the segment under both metrics.
Lead vehicle braked twice late in the segment while follower clearance remained under 3 s, demonstrating the practical risk of the short following distance.
Safe-T-Cam enforcement zone, indicating this corridor is specifically monitored for following-distance compliance.

mitigating_factors.factor: No sustained or acute closing hazard was detected (ttc_s null, seconds_closing = 0.0), suggesting a steady rather than escalating risk.
Absolute speeds were low (mean follower speed 27.2 km/h, well under the 100 km/h limit), meaning required stopping distances in metres were correspondingly short despite the sub-threshold time gap.
Road surface was dry, partially offsetting (though not eliminating) the night-time visibility concern that drives the stricter 4 s calibration.
4 of 95 samples were excluded for low confidence, introducing minor uncertainty into the sustained-duration figures.

verdict.counterfactual: If the 4 low-confidence excluded samples had actually shown clearance_s consistently above 4 s (e.g. the gap had stabilised earlier), sustained_clearance_below_3s_seconds would likely drop below the ~5 s transiency threshold and the verdict would weaken to possible_breach.
verdict.explanation_for_lay_user: The camera data shows the following car stayed unusually close to the car in front - only about 1.8 to 2.0 seconds of clear road on average - for most of a 5-second window at night, when drivers are legally expected to leave at least 4 seconds. This pattern held up whether you measure from bumper-to-bumper or account for the following car's own length, so the conclusion doesn't depend on which method you trust. There's no sign the driver was actively speeding up to close the gap dangerously, and the actual speeds involved were low, which is some mitigation, but the sustained short gap at night still points to a likely Rule 126 breach.
